WITH BLOODHOUNDS.
Exciting Chase After Two Negro Burglar.

BRUNSON'S, S.C., Feb. 21.—An exciting chase of two negroes with bloodhounds occurred near here last night. Tom Brounell and Bob Riching, two negro men, broke in a store near Brunson's, Saturday night, and carried off about one hundred dollars' worth of goods. These two men were at once suspicioned of the robbery. Last night it was understood that they were making their way down the Brunson turnpike in the direction of Columbia. A party was quickly organized and mounted. Five bloodhounds were procured and pursuit of the negroes begun.

The road is a level and beautiful one. The men were all mounted, and the dogs thoroughly trained. They quickly found the scent of the fleeing negroes, and it was followed with savage delight. As the scent became warmer and warmer the hounds became wild with ferocious delight, and sprang forward at a speed rarely ever seen. The hunters followed close behind. After a race or three miles the fleeing darkles were sighted by the dogs. They bounded over the smooth surface at an increased rate. Their wild yelps made cold chills run through the negroes, who, however, determined to give them a race. They are athletic, and considered the best pedestrians in the country.

With the five baying bloodhounds at their heels, they sped on. Despite the desperate efforts they made, and the fearful rate at which they fairly flew over the ground, the animals rapidly gained on their prey. As they ascended a slight hill two of them pounced upon the fugitives. As they throw them to the ground the hunters came up and arrested the negroes, who were promptly put in jail. The chase was an exciting one, and joined in by several persons along the road.

GREENSBORO, N. C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. This morning as Lizzie Fluch, a little 10-year-old daughter of Mrs. Jennie Fluch, living near Hillsboro, was on her way to the spring, she was accosted by William Gauch, a negro of bad character. The second made an infamous proposal to the girl, who, frightened by the look in his eyes, attempted to run away. He caught her and committed a rape upon her person. He at once died, and the child now lies in a precarious condition. Citizens of the county are looking for him.

Intelligence has reached here also of an infamous offense of a similar nature at Martinsville yesterday evening. Charles Gilmor, a negro, actually went into the house of Mr. Prince Winchester, white he and his wife were absent. The sole occupant of the house at the time was Miss Winchester. Knowing Gilmor, she asked him what he wanted, and suspecting that he had crept into the house for the purpose of robbery, she ordered him out. The negro, glaring boldly at her, told her he had no idea of leaving yet, and then went on to tell her to keep quiet on pain of death. At once guessing his horrible design, the young woman began to scream for help. Gilmor attempted to commit his devilish design upon her person, and despite her great struggles would have accomplished his purpose had he not been frightened off by the sound of footsteps of neighbors attracted by the girl's screams. He barely had time to leap from the rear window before they entered the house. Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day. This is the third offense of this character committed by Gilmor. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. He was a few years after convicted of rape and sentenced to twenty years in the Penitentiary, but after serving nine years he was released.

IN MEMORIAM.
Death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer—Meeting of the Official Board of Tryon Street Church, Charlotte.

The recent death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer, late of Edenton Street Church, Raleigh, former pastor of Tryon Street Charlotte, has affected the hearts of his former charge with deepest sorrow, and is felt in the whole community. During his pastoral charge of Tryon Street Church, through a period of four years, his ministry was marked by gentleness, faithfulness and ability—the most perfect esteem, affection, and confidence of his flock was maintained, while not a single discord occurred to mar the harmony of the relation between pastor and people.

The impress that he left upon this community was only for good. The fervency of his piety, the purity of, and transparency of his character, the simplicity and geniality of his social life, and the attractiveness of his preaching made him a general favorite in his own Church and won the admiration and esteem of the community.

Richly endowed with these qualities, he was prepared to be a "workman that need not be ashamed"—a faithful shepherd to those "over whom the Holy Ghost made him overseer"—a "wise master-builder" in the temple of the Lord—attractive and loving in the social circle, patient toward the erring, kind and tender in the sick room and house of mourning.

Deeply impressed with his character, we are deeply affected by his early death. We feel that we and the whole Church have suffered a great loss. We feel that the grief of his family is our grief, and the grief of the Church.

Hence, as we are bowed with a common sorrow, we mingle our tears with theirs. While wife, and father, and mother, and child, sit solitary in the shadow of this great grief, our hearts not only feel a kindred pang, but respond in sympathy and condolence to the appeal that comes from bleeding hearts.

Again we are impressed with the inscrutable mystery of Providence in removing a life so full of promise to the Church, just as it was approximating its prime, while there are so many waste places uncultivated and harvests ungathered. The workmen fall, still work goes on. The soldier dies at his post, still the battle does not cease; nor are the banners furled. "God buries His workmen, but carries on His work." So is it ever. We reverence this wisdom. We bow to this power. We adore this goodness. We are subdued under a sense of infinity!

While we stand with uncovered head in the presence of the Disposer of events, and bow our hearts in profoundest grief, we recognize in it the special providence of God, who is "too wise to err and too good to be unkind." Thus endeavoring to submit to the supreme decision of the Head of the Church, and to acquiesce in all the developments of His providence, we, the officers of Tryon Street Church, representing in this case the sentiments of the whole Church, while expressing our own sorrow at the death of our former pastor and friend, desire most heartily and sincerely to express to the bereaved family of the deceased our deepest sympathy; and we do most devoutly pray that God, in whose service he lived, labored, and died, may communicate to them His richest consolations in this trying hour, and so sanctify this afflictive dispensation of His providence as that it shall prove to them a blessing, both for time and eternity.

It was ordered that this communication be sent to the Charlotte papers and Raleigh Christian Advocate for publication—also that a copy be sent to Mrs. A. A. Boshamer as a testimony of our sympathy and affectionate regard.

CHARLESTON, S. C., April 14 — The barn of J. S. Blalock, at Martin's Depot, in Laurens county, was burnt on the 3d instant. Lynch Law.

There is no State in the Union, in which this old time method of met ing out justice to criminals is not resorted to in cases of heinous crimes committed with premeditation and under circumstances of great aggravation. With the progress of law and civilization it is rarely exercised though common in wild and newly settled regions. In a country like ours it is never excusable, though cases arise, at times, which seem to call for swifter punishment than is obtainable under the slow process of law. In no case do we believe that calm reflection will approve lynch law, not only because it is a violation of law, but because innocent life may be taken under the excitement created by an atrocious crime. We have judges, jurors and all officials necessary to the punishment of crime, and the enforcement of law according to law has a wholesome influence on society, while the violation of law has a demoralizing tendency. A case of lynching a negro woman occurred in Laurens County, two miles above Clinton on the 9th instant. The barn of Mr. Blalock had been set on fire and burned on the 3d instant and the barn was so near the dwelling house that it was considered an attempt to burn it also. Suspicion pointed to Judy Metts, a negro woman living on his place, and who had been charged two years ago with burning the dwelling of Mr. Simpson. On the 9th a warrant was sworn out against her and on Saturday night she was arrested by a constable, who started with her for Clinton. About two miles from Martin's Depot a party of disguised men took both the constable and prisoner in charge, and while some retained the constable others took off the prisoner. On Sunday morning her body was found hanging to a tree about 200 yards from the point the lynchers took her in charge. At the inquest on Monday the coroner's jury returned a verdict that she came to her death by hanging, at the hands of parties unknown. No one has been arrested and so far none of the party is known. While arson is a high crime, punishable with death, unless the jury recommend the party to mercy, still it is not of a character to call for lynching, especially when the building was not a dwelling house. To permit such highhanded violations of law in such cases tends to disorganize society and government and to lead people to become judges and executioners in all cases. When the crime is horrible as in rape and murder combined &c., then much allowance can be made for over excitement and ultra legal remedies, but in this case no such excuse exists.

cowan-martins-depot-1881-04-09.A27:
A Woman Hanged by a Mob in Laurens County.
The habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes in this State has gone on constantly for several years, and without censure, but now we are glad to see that two or three journals of the State have had the manhood to denounce the recent hanging of the half-witted negro woman in Laurens county.—Abbeville Press and Banner.

The hanging of this woman by a mob can not be too severely condemned, and we trust the officers of the law in Laurens County will ferret out the guilty parties and have them punished according to the enormity of their crime. The zeal of our esteemed contemporary in this direction is to be commended, but when it accuses the people of the State of "the habit of lynching weak and defeseless negroes," we think it is going farther than the facts will justify. The only lynching in the State that we remember, up to the time of the lynching of this woman, was for the heinous offense of rape and murder. The first fiend who met the vengeance of an outraged community for rape, was John J. Moore, a white man in Spartanburg county. Then followed the lynching of three negroes in Clarendon county for the brutal murder of a white woman and plundering of the house, and the lynching of the two negro brutes at Prosperity for the outrage and murder of Miss Wertz.

The indiscrtminate charge of murder and lawlessness against our people is common with the Radical sheets of the North, but the Press and Banner is the first Democratic paper in the State, or the South, which has made a similar charge. It would have been better for the good reputation of our contemporary to have given the number of "weak and defenseless negroes" lynched, and the character of the offenses for which they were lynched. Messrs. Baldwin & Co., of the Eureka Guano Manufacturing Company of Orient, L. L., will commence at once the erection of a large guano factory at Port Royal. The works and sheds will cover ten acres of ground, and will have a water frontage on Battery river of two thousand one hundred feet. The works are to be completed and in operation August 1.

The Governor has received the report of the jury of inquest on the Laurens lynching case, and immediately offered a reward of two hundred dollars for the apprehension of each of the persons engaged in the affair. As some thirty men are supposed to have had a hand in it, the reward will very likely stimulate some detective to work up the case.

The Richland Light Dragoons of Columbia are pressing forward their preparations for their grand tournament and ball, to take place on the 9th of May. The tilt will take place at the Fair Grounds, and will begin at 3 o'clock p. m.

George T. Graham, Thomas S. Arthur and Noah Corley, of Lexington, were before Commissioner Stoeber, last week, charged with election offenses. The former waived examination and gave bond, and the two latter were held for trial.

The fishing smack Mary Alice, Capt. Jackson Grant, was capsized off the bar at Charleston Saturday by a sudden flaw of wind, and the whole of the crew, consisting of the Captain and three colored men, were precipitated into the water. The Captain and two of the men succeeded in holding on to the boat, but the third man, Jacob Green, was swept off by a wave, and before assistance came was carried out of sight. The other men were brought to the city in another fishing boat.

General John S. Preston died on Sunday morning at his residence in Columbia, of cirrhosis of the liver. He had been sinking from day to day and his death was expected. His wife and two daughters, his brother, Col. Thomas Preston, and others of his family were at his bedside. He was buried in Trinity Churchyard, Columbia, on Tuesday. He was the brother of Senator Wm. C. Preston, and was born in Abingdon, Virginia, in 1809. In 1831 he married Miss Caroline Hampton, step-aunt of Senator Hampton. He rendered good service in the late war, but his splendid property was sadly wrecked during the struggle, and under the carpet-bag regime. He was widely known and universally respected.

A very severe storm passed through the lower portion of Sumter county last week, doing very considerable damage to fences, timber and buildings. Buildings were moved and unroofed in one or two localities.

Mr. Charles Vardel, assistant superintendent at the tea farm near Summerville, has on exhibition a number of interesting relics, which were unearthed while making explorations in the basement of the old colonial building on the farm. Some rare china and porcelain vessels, a beautiful vase, and a design in terra cotta are among the best preserved specimens. The rest have been badly injured by the fire which destroyed the building many years ago.

The State Superintendent of Education, Col. H. S. Thompson, has decided to hold a normal school this summer for colored teachers, such as was held last year for white, and will be repeated this. He is in correspondence with an experienced instructor in that branch of education, and when he has consulted with him in regard to his other engagements he will appoint a time and place for the meeting.

At a late meeting of the Board of County Commissioners of Beaufort county a resolution was passed that "outside paupers be stricken from the list and that the inmates of the alms house be only such as are sick, indigent and without relatives to aid in their support." This action was taken on account of the reduced revenue of the county resulting from the abolition of the license system. It was estimated that the cost of supporting the paupers would amount to $3,500 per annum at the present rate of expenditure.

The Rev. T. P. Bell, of Anderson, and the Rev. John Stout, of Society Hill, both young and talented ministers of the Baptist Church, have tendered their services to the Board of Foreign Missions of the Southern Baptist Church for missionary work in China. Their services have been accepted by the board and they will depart for their field of labor in October.

The Clarendon Enterprise says: "The approach of the Cowpens Centennial celebration brings to mind the fact that the wife of our highly esteemed fellow-citizen, Mr. Arthur Harvin, is one of a few living descendants of William Maybin, one of the heroes of that battle. On one occasion Mr. Maybin was taken prisoner and carried to Charleston, S.C., where he soon after died on board a British prison ship, one of those channel houses of liberty. His wife's brother, Benjamin Duncan, a soldier in the British army, obtained permission to bring his corpse on shore for burial. Duncan then visited his bereaved sister. Upon returning to his duty, Duncan promised to come back as soon as possible, leaving a watch and other things as a pledge. This watch is now in the possession of Mrs. Arthur Harvin, by whom it is highly prized."

The annual meeting of the South Carolina State Press Association will begin to-day at Beaufort. The citizens of the town have made ample preparations for the reception and entertainment of the delegates. The following committees have been appointed: On arrangements—Dr. H. M. Stewart, Wm. Elliott, Rev. John Kershaw, H. S. Elliott, P. M. Whitman and W. H. Calvert; on finances—Geo. Waterhouse and Wm. H. Lockwood; on conferring with the citizens of Port Royal—John Conant and H. S. Elliott. An address of welcome to the association will be made by Col. William Elliott on Wednesday. In the evening the members of the association will be serenaded. The Greenville Incendiaries.

In another column we give some particulars of the conviction and sentence of the Greenville incendiaries. These degrees have been twice convicted of burning valuable property in the city of Greenville, and twice the sentence of death has been pronounced upon four of the parties charged with the crime. The Supreme Court granted a new trial in the first instance, and that tribunal will again be appealed to in their behalf. As to the probable result of that appeal none can foretell.

The trial of men for their lives always develops in the public mind a feeling of interest, and, no matter how guilty the accused may be, there is, in the hearts of those far away from the aggravating scenes, a feeling of sympathy for those who may be sentenced to death, and the mind naturally runs over any facts which may excite a doubt as to the guilt of the accused, or which may exhibit any unusual zeal on the part of the all-powerful Government in its efforts, under the forms of law, to put one of its citizens to death. The money of the Government to employ detectives we presume was not spared in this particular case, and the detectives for their energy and fidelity to the work which they had undertaken deserve commendation. The Governor also has shown a commendable interest in the matter, and in order to make competent the testimony of Fletcher Maddux, that officer showed his interest in the matter when he pardoned him out of the penitentiary and removed his disabilities, incurred by other felonies for the express purpose of convicting his comrades or associates in crime. And then as the crowning act in this drama, which is to end in a tragedy, besides an able and efficient Soliciter, Mr. M. F. Ansel, one of the best lawyers in Greenville, and Col. W. E. Earle, formerly of Greenville, but now of Washington, D. C., were employed to assist the State in the prosecution. Everybody knows that no man in upper South Carolina wields a greater influence before a jury than Colonel Earle. With an array of counsel like this, when it is remembered that one criminal was pardoned out of the penitentiary to get sufficient evidence to convict, and the zeal of the detectives is fresh in our minds, it is easily to be seen that the State has done its whole duty in its efforts to convict these men, and if it were customary for the State so to act, it would not now be a matter of note. As evidence of the extraordinary zeal manifested to convict these men, we may be pardoned for referring to the murder of Judy Metts, in Laurens where, it is supposed five, or six, or possibly eight, white men hanged this negro in the night time. If any effort, except the offering of a reward by the Governor, has been made to arrest the perpetrators of this crime, we have not heard of it. In this we would not blame our most excellent Governor, because we know that he cannot do much to correct evil, except where he has the aid and sympathy of the community in which crime has been committed. We presume that nobody in Laurens county wants to see respectable white men hanged for the murder of a Judy Metts, who was a half-crazy negro, and, as a matter of course, friendless. The Greenville incendiaries committed their offence against the sentiment of a powerful community, who will be able to have the offenders punished.

We put fault at no man's door in this matter, nor do we blame the Government at all. The fact is, we merely remark upon a state of society which punishes one class of criminals to the full extent of the law, while another class need not fear being brought into court.

Now, for the condemned men at Greenville: In the first place they had no money to employ counsel, and had to accept such services as lawyers were willing to render without pay. Solicitor Orr in open court, when speaking of their lawyers, pronounced the leading counsel which they had, as not "responsible for what he said, but regarded him as a crazy man."

We suppose that three stronger men could not have appeared for the State than Orr, Ansel, and Earle. Taking the State Solicitor's remarks about the defendants council as true, the contest seems to have been an unequal one, and, no matter how guilty, we confess our sympathy for men convicted and sentenced to death under circumstances like these.

Railroad Accident.

BOSTON, December 31.—A special engine with caboose, running west on the New York and New England road collided with the east-bound local train near Thompson, Conn., this afternoon. The engineer had been ordered to keep out of the way of the passenger train, but the orders seem to have been forgotten, and the special proceeded on to the other train's time. W. P. A Sensation in Colorado—Murder and Suicide.

LEADVILLE, December 4th.—Gold Park mining camp is in a furure of excitement. Four days ago Henry Weston, foreman of the Gold Park Mining Company, was shot and killed by one Bagley, a discharged blacksmith. Bagley also made an unsuccessful attempt to shoot Superintendent Turney. He then fortified himself in a cabin, which was immediately surrounded by a mob. The cabin was beigeed for eight hours without dislodging the occupant. Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited. The explosion following tore the cabin to pieces, and Bagley was found with a bullet hole through his heart, having evidently committed suicide. Bagley has several sympathizers, who have threatened Turney's life, and a strong guard surrounds his cabin day and night. Jack White and Bagley's friends were ordered out of the camp by the Vigilantes, and paraded the town all day with a pair of cocked revolvers looking for the committee, but left at night. Much trouble is anticipated.

Repenting at Leisure.

NEW YORK, December 3d.—The evening papers have the following: About two years ago the daughter of Amos Stillman, of Brooklyn, eloped with W. S. Guild. Miss Stillman was only about 16, while Guild was 70. After a private marriage ceremony, they slipped away to Europa without the knowledge of relations or friends. Things were not just what the young bride thought they would be, and in four days she became home-sick and prevailed upon Guild to return. When they reached the wharf in New York he hired a coach and sent her home to her parents, while he got upon another steamer and set sail for California. For one year he remitted the young bride $10 per week, and then the remittance stopped. Now she sues him for a limited divorce on the ground of abandonment. It is understood that he claims she abandoned him. This morning a motion was made by her counsel for counsel fees and alimony. It was opposed by the counsel for defendant, who said his client was in California, and he would have to send affidavits to him. The case was postponed.

A Bold Bond Robbery.

CLEVELAND (O.), December 31.—A daring theft captured a box from the Commercial National Bank, containing $117,000 in bonds. They were Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad, Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad, Chicago and Atchison Bridge Company bonds. The man had been sitting in the office, and when the coupon cutting was finished and the bonds replaced in the box, he quickly whisked the box from the table and disappeared, being gone half an hour before the bonds were missed. President D. P. Eell was responsible for the careless manner in which the securities were exposed. The bonds are all negotiable. The man was short and stout, with short-cropped whiskers.

Lost In the Snow.

DENVER, December 31.—A Tribune's special from Durango says: A man named Moyle, two brothers named Chapman, and two others, names unknown, several days ago left Ophir to walk to Silverton, and have not been heard from since. The snow on the range is over three feet deep, and it is believed they perished. A party has gone in search.

Catholic Priest Shot.

SPRINGFIELD (Mass.), December 4th.—The wife of David McMillan left him several years ago. Lately she became housekeeper for Father McCarthy, parish priest at Greenfield. Last night McMillan went to the parsonage, but was refused admittance. He returned three times and rang the door-bell violently and kicked the door, and when Father McCarthy came to the door McMillan shot him twice, and he was fatally wounded.

Death Rather than Murriage.

FLUSHING (N. Y.), December 4th—George Wiggins, compelled by the Court to marry, entered a field, strapped a gun to the fence, and standing in front discharged the piece by a string, and was instantly killed.

National Banks.

WASHINGTON, December 4th—Comptroller Knox, in his report, says that 86 national banks were organized during the year ending November 1st last, with an aggregate authorized capital of $9,651,050, to which $5,233,580 in circulating notes have been issued. This is the largest number of banks organized in any year since 1872.

Father McCarthy's Assailant—Lodged in Greenfield Jail—The Wounded Priest Past Recovery.
GREENFIELD, Dec. 6.—David McMillan, who shot Father McCarthy, reached Greenfield at 6:45 to night in charge of Officer Fitzgerald. Fears were entertained of an attempt on the part of some of the enraged parishioners of Father McCarthy to lynch the prisoner, and by permission of Assistant Superintendent Turner of the Fitchburg road the train was stopped some one hundred rods, below the depot, and the prisoner with Officer Fitzgerald and another officer was taken into a carriage and driven rapidly to the jail. News of this plan had, however, in some way leaked out and the yard before the jail was crowded with people anxious to get at the prisoner. A committee from the Catholic church was, however, present and assisted the officers in preserving order and guarding the prisoner. The crowd was in earnest and closed around the team with shouts of "Pull him out!" "Pull him out." "Shoot the villain!" but the gleaming revolvers of the officers deterred them from any actual application of force. McMillan was thoroughly frightened and fairly dragged the officer to whom he was handeuffed up the jail steps in his terror lest the crowd should seize him. He will be examined at noon to-morrow at the jail before Trial Justice Thompson on a complaint charging him with intent to kill. Father McCarthy, the wounded priest, passed a bad night Monday and grew worse to day until late in the afternoon, when his physicians gave up hope of his recovery. Should he die before Wednesday noon McMillan will be arraigned on a charge of murder.

Fools and Damphools.
The world has agreed for the sake of convenience to divide its fools into two species. One it calls simply a fool; the other, to adopt the word which Doesticks applied to his friend, it calls a damphool. This is used strictly in its scientific, not its profane, and has nothing in common with the shallow and random use which angry men make of it to give vent to their momentary irritation. It is as distinct and technical a label as "mustang" to describe a species of horse, or "terrier" to describe a species of dog.

A fool is often harmless, and may be snubbed and kept in order. A damphool cannot be. A fool is often tolerable and docile. If he cannot be taught much wisdom, he can be taught obedience and respect. But though a damphool may have intelligence, he has little or no reverence. A fool may have some humor, but a damphool has none. A tool can be made a fool of; a damphool makes a fool of himself. A fool may have a little sense, but whatever other sense a damphool may possess, he is sure to lack common sense. A fool may be humble and retiring, but it is the essence of his kinsmen to be conceited and self-asserting. A fool generally knows he is a fool, and so is often doleful when he thinks of it; but a damphool never knows it, and so is happy. A fool is often stupid, headless, blundering, aimless, like a hen or a fly; the other is strutting, irritating, conceited, like a turkey and a peacock; or a noisy nuisance, like a June beetle. A fool is often patient, well-digposed, and, though slow, good-natured, like the ass; but his foster brother is apt to bear malice, and is intelligently obstinate like the mule.

To the ranks of the odious kind of fool belong those who hanker morbidly for notoriety—the Tanners, the Bradlaughs, the Guiteaus, the Booths, the Count Johannes and George Francis Trains. Poor Train, however, has stepped down and out of the ranks, and now appears to be simply and only a fool. The fool is an object of sympathy, of pity, compassion and help; his robust relative gives cause for disgust, for sport, for derision and ridicule. Shakspeare, of course, saw the difference between these types, and has drawn them with his usual clearness and acuteness. His fools and clowns are famous—Touchstone and Dogberry; Launce, Slender old Gobbo, and the like; but his damphools—such as Justice Shallow, Pistol, Falstaff, Polonious, old Capulet, have equal rights to consideration. When, in the play of “Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the dramatist changed Bottom the Weaver into an ass, he turned his damphool into a simple fool. For Bottom the Weaver imagines he can write a play, take the chief role and be stage manager all at the same time, making himself poussed and ridiculous, indeed; but changed into an ass he is docile and humble and wants only to have his head scratched and to be fed on dried peas and good sweet hay.

A fool may be pious and reverential, believe in creeds and religion; but the other sort is quite likely to be an atheist. David undoubtedly meant to write that the damphool “hath said there is no God.”

A BRUTE LYNCHED.—A Paducah (Ky.) special says that on August 9 E. Reeves, colored, attempted indecent violence on the person of Miss Dora Lingston, in Graves county, having broken into the room in the night. Her cries brought help, and he fled. Gately, who was arrested at Dedham, Mass., for the murder of his wife, has made a confession, stating that she angered him and that he beat her with a stick, which he afterwards threw away. He did not intend to kill her, he says. They hang such fellows as he in Massachusetts.

A bloody double tragedy occurred at the town of Burton, Mo., on the Wabash railroad, on Wednesday. A man named Jackson insulted a lady named Langford. The lady told her husband, who at once hunted up Jackson, and began chastising him. Jackson drew a knife and stabbed Langford several times, inflicting mortal wounds. Mrs Langford then appeared on the scene and shot Jackson in the breast, whereupon he turned on the woman, cut her slightly two or three times, when he fell exhausted from loss of blood. Both Jackson and Langford will die.

Benjamin Bird (colored), convicted of the murder of Policeman Nelson (colored) June 25, 1880, during the mill riot at Jacksonville, Fla., was executed at 12 o'clock, Friday, in the jail yard. A short time previous to the execution he made a confession of the crime to the sheriff and others, but while on the gallows protested his innocence. When the trap was sprung and Bird fell, the noose had not been properly arranged, the end slipped out and he fell to the ground. He got up with the assistance of the sheriff, and again walked upon the trap, the rope being properly adjusted, and he was launched into eternity.

James and Walter Malley have been arrested at New Haven charged with the murder of Jennie E. Cramer, the young girl whose death has produced such a sensation in the city of elms. Blanche Douglass made a confession before the coroner's jury at Sheriff Peck's house, Tuesday night, regarding the death of Jennie Cramer. She says that on Friday night she was called into the room occupied by James Malley and Jennie Cramer, to quiet Jennie, who was screaming and pleading with James Malley. At midnight she was still in consultation with the jury, but nothing further was elicited. The citizens of Orange, in town meeting Tuesday afternoon, voted to offer a reward of $1000 for evidence enough to convict the murderer or murderess of Jennie Cramer.

The town of Dedham, Mass.. was the scene of a murder, Wednesday night. Patrick Gately and his wife, Mary, live in the east part of Dedham. Mrs Gately was the victim, and her husband's story is that she complained of feeling unwell, about 7:30 o'clock, and that she went to bed. Next foren o1, about 5 o'clock, he called her, but got no answer. He went into her room and found that the whole left side of her was crushed in and marks of violence all over her body. The bed was stained with blood, and there was evidence of a violent struggle. The walls and ceiling was also stained with blood. Her husband has been arrested for the crime, and the clothes that he wore have the appearance of having been washed. His handkerchief also contained brook sand. A medical examiner will hold an autopsy. Gately is about forty years old. There is great excitement. Gately protests his innocence.

N. H. N. G. Encampment.

The annual encampment of the first brigade of the New Hampshire National Guard will be held on the land of Mrs Rowe, about a mile north of West Concord village, just above the fork of the roads, commencing Tuesday, September 13, and continuing four days. —Two little boys, aged about seven and
eight years respectively, were playing in the street on Washington avenue near Nineteenth street yesterday evening about four o'clock, when one of them was attacked by a ferocious bore hog. The beast grabbed the child in the calf of the leg and while lacerating it the other little fellow picked up a stick and rushed to the rescue when the beast suddenly turned upon him, caught his arm and buried his teeth in the flesh. The cries of the lads attracted the attention of passers by, and Mr. Eberly, who was among the first to notice the trouble, hurried to the assistance of the boys and rescued them from their perilous predicament. As it is, both boys received very painful wounds, but they might have been crippled for life. The beast should be hunted down and killed and the ordinance against bore hogs in general be rigidly enforced.

CHICAGO, March 7.—The State board of agriculture of Illinois having recently strongly recommended Emory Cobb, of this State, for commissioner of agriculture, that action was speedily followed by nearly every other board in the northwestern States, and by prominent newspapers, including the Chicago Tribune, Evening Journal, Prairie Farmer and the National Live Stock Journal. The latter paper says the office of commissioner has since its creation been a sort of harbor for seedy politicians, and still remains a chaotic, unorganized, aimless, worthless affair, and so it will remain until, by a stroke of good fortune, a strong man, with first-class executive ability, thorough business training and an intimate practical acquaintance with the agricultural interests of our country shall be placed at its head. With such a man it might be a power in the councils of our nation. Without disparaging the abilities of the others who are named for the position, the Journal has no hesitation in affirming its conviction that Mr. Cobb is, above all that have been suggested, the man for the place, and this conviction is strongly held by all who know him.

MISS ISHMAEL AVENGED.
A Mysterious Mob Appears at Midnight and Hangs Her Supposed Murderers on a Tree.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 11.—The soquel to the tragic murder of Miss Ishmael, near Jonesboro, Craighhead County, was learned to-day. The nogroes arrested on suspicion of the murder were Green Harris, John Woods, Olles Beck, and Burt Harkins. The were examined at New Haven Church, seven miles north of Jonesboro, before Justices of the Peace Akors and Jackson, and by them committed and ordered to jail to await the action of the Grand Jury at the approaching Circuit Court. Pending their removal to prison the prisoners were placed in the church under a strong guard, the intention being to lodge them in the Jonesboro Jail early the next morning. The examination drew together hundreds of people, and the excited crowd swarmed into the church during the examination of the accused or gathered on the grounds without the cellar discussing the tragedy in low, significant tones. The examination occupied some time, and night had fallen over it was concluded, when the prisoners had been disposed of as before stated, and the people began to withdraw.

Threats had been made of lynching, but many influential planters discounted such proceeding, urging that the law, if allowed to take its course, would avenge the crime. It was supposed that their counsel had effect, and that the prisoners would be dispatched by legal means. The guards around the church were doubled however, in anticipation of mob violence. This anticipation was unhappily realized. About the hour of midnight, when the guards were beginning to feel drowsy, they were aroused by the sound of approaching footsteps, which came from the vicinity of the adjacent woods.

The next instant, as if by magic, a crowd of masked men, variously estimated at from 200 to 300, sprang out from the shadows of the trees and, surrounding the church, dominated the prisoners. The request not being complied with, the guards were overpowered in a twinkling, the doors and windows of the rude frame building smashed in, and the terrified negroes dragged out and hustled to the nearest tree. The prisoners begged piteously for their lives, but their captors were deaf to all entreaty, and in less than fifteen minutes after their capture the four negroes were dangling in the

air in the agonies of death, all having been suspended on one and the same tree.

Having completed their ghastly work the lynchers alitently dispersed, leaving the bodies of their victims still hanging, and presenting a horrid spectacle in the pale moonlight, as the night winds awayed them to and fro. It is said that all the negroes confessed their guilt before they were hanged. The excitement in the vicinity of the scene has subsided. The better class of planters depreciate the means employed for the punishment of the crime, though they hold that the murderers of Miss Ishmael deserved swift justice.

West Virginia and the Mother State.

If there is any one point upon which the people of this State are substantially of one mind it is as to the perpetual separate Stateship of West Virginia. For many years there has not been a single public man, or a journal of any creed or party, that has expressed any inclination for a reunion. Even the border-line feeling in favor of it that was manifested in Greenbrier County just after the close of the War seems to have died out. At least we hear nothing more of it. The sense of a long course of injustice toward the people of West Virginia on the part of the old State, when we were a part of it, is still alive in this State among the older people, outside of any question of politics, and the younger generation have no traditions that are not West Virginian in their character. We are all looking forward hopefully to the day when West Virginia will be developed by railroads and be made one of the most prosperous States of the Union. The more the public know of the resources of West Virginia the more they realize that she has

the elements of a great future as a State. We do not want, therefore, to be hampered by any adverse policy, such as that which kept us back under the old régime, when the public money represented in the debt of Virginia was spent almost exclusively for the development of the territory outside of our borders.

GARRISON'S GRIT.

A Little "Sand" and a Handy Revolver Saved Him a Lynching—His Explanation of the Trouble with the Grangers and His Account of the Fire in the Cheese Factory.

Young Garrison, the Winfield cheesemaker, whose arrest for alleged incendiarism and whose narrow escape from a lynching at the hands of his angry creditors were referred to in a dispatch in yesterday's Tribune, was brought before the Justice of the Peace at Wheaton yesterday, and obtained a continuance until tomorrow. Young Garrison's explanation is that it had been customary to collect money for his patrons and hold it over from time to time, and no trouble had ever come of it until now. The reason he had not paid dividends to the Winfield farmers was that some of his October collections were behind, and he desired to make as large a payment as possible. The claims ranged from $20 to $500, and aggregated several thousand dollars. He had promised his patrons to pay them on Thursday last, and had on hand for that purpose $7,000 in greenbacks. Not desiring to keep this large sum in one place, where burglaries could get it in case they should raid the establishment, he divided it into three parcels, and hid it in a room on the second floor of the factory on Wednesday night. He then, in company with Mr. Frank Burroughs, the young man who was working in the factory, retired. They slept in an adjoining room, on the second floor, in which were their clothes and the books of the concern. About midnight Burroughs was aroused by a peculiar noise, and going to a window he discovered that

THE BOILER-ROOM WAS WRAPPED IN FLAMES
and the factory itself was being rapidly consumed. He roused Garrison, and they immediately endeavored to get into the adjoining room and secure the money they had placed there earlier in the evening, but it was too late. The room was filled with flame and smoke, and the floor and roof soon fell in. They seized a trunk of Garrison's and got it out of the building, but failed to secure anything else. The next day young Garrison was arrested for arson at the instance of some of his patrons, but before he could be taken to Wheaton, the farmers who had waited so patiently for their money heard of the occurrence of the night before and flocked to the scene in a very angry mood. A large number of these people had collected, and as their losses occurred to them they became enraged beyond control. Some one suggested that they hang him, and a rope was speedily procured, and the crowd started for the station where young Garrison was. When questioned on this point he admitted it to be true, and being asked what saved his neck, he replied, "If it had not been for a little 'sand' and a revolver in my pocket I would have been strung up." It appears, however, that Judge Drummond, who lives near Winfield, came on the scene at this time, and doubtless his presence had much to do toward pacifying the enraged farmers.

CHICAGO, November 28, 1881.

Corruption in Chicago courts received a death blow to-day at the hands of Judge Tuley, of the criminal bench. He dismissed a whole panel of jurors. Why? Simply because he considered those composing it to be men unworthy to act impartially. He avowed his purpose not to accept as a juror a man not of the highest reputation for integrity. This is a move in the right direction, and Judge Tuley deserves the greatest praise for taking the initiative in this much needed reform; but it is to be hoped that the bench throughout the city, and the whole country, will be influenced to adopt the same salutary measures.

Rowell, the great English pedestrian, is in Chicago. He considers young Dobler, of Chicago, the second best walker in the world. They are matched to walk at no far distant day.

The Pennsylvania railroad has commenced a prosecuting war on the "scalpers." How very strange it is that none of the "scalpers" are ever prosecuted successfully. A friend at my elbow intimates that the several railroads may, periodically, when passenger travel is light and funds short, "unload" tickets to the scalpers. By this dodge persons who could not pay full fare would be induced to buy low priced tickets. Thus an impetus would be given to travel and expenses to rolling stock be paid, while the regular full fare traffic would not be injured. My friend may be right. If so, then this hurrah against the poor scalper is all buncombe.

The Jews of Chicago are organizing for the relief of their brethren who are being driven from Russia, and who are coming to Chicago. This is a praiseworthy move.

CHICAGO, March 12.—Thirty-one persons, including several women, have been arrested at Palestine, Ohio, a little town near the Indiana line, for sending threatening letters to Jacob Long, a saloon keeper. Baroness Burdett-Coutts, who married Mr. Ashmoad Bartlett, formerly of Philadelphia, is coming over to see her American collateral relatives.

BARNES' BAD BREAK.
His Crookedness Causes Him to be Strung Up by a Masked Mob.
He Was to Have Been Married in Sedalia on Tuesday Evening Last.
In Tuesday's BAZOO brief mention was made that the store of Frank M. Stotts, at Prairie Ridge, Saline county, had been entered Sunday evening, the 4th inst., by a burglar, who had secured $150 in cash and a revolver, but had subsequently been arrested, having been traced by tracks in the snow. The thief proved to be a man named Thos. Barnes, a traveling photographer, who had been doing business for a month or so in a tent in Prairie Ridge, having come to that place from Pilot Grove, Cooper county.

Yesterday Mr. Stotts, the gentleman whose money was stolen, was in Sedalia and gave the BAZOO a call. He related a story in connection with the affair that is full of interest.

After: satisfying himself that Barnes was the thief, he placed him under arrest, and word was sent to Sheriff John Cason, at Marshall, to come and get the prisoner. Although there was no positive proof against Barnes, all felt confident that he was guilty and they hit upon a novel plan to wring from him a confession.

Sam Cockrell, E. B. Ruckle, and about twenty-five others, all among the best of Saline's citizens, organized themselves into a band for that purpose, and entered into an understanding with Sheriff Cason, who was to remove the prisoner to Marshall, that on the way out the party, masked, would be lying in ambush, and have in charge another prisoner whom they would be pretending to hang, after which they would seize Barnes and go through the performance of hanging him also, and thus, if he was guilty, obtain his confession.

Thursday night, when about three miles west of Prairie Ridge, as the sheriff and his prisoner were passing on their way to Marshall, they ran across the masked party, who had in charge a man named Jasper Smith, who had been informed of what was up and had been prepared for the occasion. Straps were securely fastened under his arms, and to these the rope was attached, after which he was suspended for a brief period, Barnes, in the meantime, being in the custody of the sheriff, some thirty yards distant. After four or five minutes had elapsed, Smith was pronounced dead, when the rope was cut and he was let to the ground. Of course he had not been hurt in the least, but it had the desired effect of scaring Barnes badly; and when, a few minutes later, the mob seized and gave him to understand that he, too, must suffer death, as they knew him as one of the thieves, he weakened perceptibly. The rope was placed around his neck in anything but a gentle manner, and the supposed mob was about to proceed to work, when Barnes, frightened nigh unto death, inquired if they did not intend to give him a show for his life. He was told to proceed and tell all he knew of the burglary. At first he claimed that Jasper Smith, whom he supposed to have been hanged until dead, and another man named Joseph Smith, were implicated with him in the theft. He signified his willingness to return to Prairie Ridge and turn over a portion of the stolen money and revolver, and his offer was accepted. In charge of four guards he returned to the Ridge, when $0 of the $150 was recovered, and also the revolver. The other $80 he had lost. He was then informed of the ruse that had been played upon him, and admitted, after learning that Jasper Smith was not dead, that he alone was guilty. This was all the masked party desired, and the prisoner was again turned over to Sheriff Cason.

Friday he was removed to the jail at Marshall, and at the next term of court will receive his sentence.

It seems that Barnes was to have been married in this city on Tuesday last to a widow lady with one child, who resides in Lincoln, Benton county, and who was to have met him on that day. He was probably short of cash, and resorted to the above method of making a raise, and will now suffer the penalty of his crime.

THE LYNCHING AT QUINCY, FLA.
Graphic Description of the Hanging of Lunn Whittaker.
A Quincy Herald extra, issued on Sunday morning, gives the following additional particulars of the lynching of Lunn Whittaker:

"Some time between the hours of two and three o'clock this morning the county jail was entered by a crowd of twenty or thirty armed men, clad in blouses and well masked, who overpowered the jail guard and took a negro prisoner, Lunn Whittaker, from the room where he was confined, and proceeded with him about a quarter of a mile from the jail—into the woods just east of town—and hung him by the neck till he was dead, from a convenient limb of a black oak tree. The news of the lynching spread like wild fire. It was received with incredulity by the citizens of this law-abiding community, but a visit to the spot confirmed the fact. The work of the Vigilantes had been thoroughly though inartistically performed.

"The victim was hoisted with an ordinary plow-line, and the noose was so unscientifically adjusted—the knot tightening before touching his neck—that his suffering must have been horrible. He was a large, powerful man; had on a light colored pair of pantaloons, a dark coat, and had on one boot—a stocking only being on the other foot. The sight was a horrible one, though a large number viewed the remains.

"The guard, consisting of three or four young men of unimpeachable grit, were most unceremoniously 'bounced.' In order to relieve the motony of the situation, they were singing a song. In midst of the ditty, and before they could wink—Prestol they were surrounded, and looking down the muzzles of cocked navy revolvers—an average of about four pistols to each guard. Resistance would have been mere insanity. They were forced to accompany the lynchers, and witnessed the choking. The men were in dead earnest, and 'meant business' from the word 'go.' McJunkin's assassination."

BOUND TO HANG HICKS,
A Mob Visits Covington for the Purpose of Lynching a Murderer, but is Repealed.
A Mob Visits Covington for the Purpose of Lynching a Murderer, but is Repulsed.

Covington, December 17.—A crowd of one hundred and fifty or two hundred men gathered in a barn to-night to lynch the negro Hicks, now in jail charged with the murder of Henry Williams. Marshal Goodson placed the prisoner in the most secure cell in the jail and brought his police force in, fifteen men, and arming them heavily with revolvers, stationed them so as to command only the entrance to the jail, besides he organized a force of fifteen citizens armed with guns, to patrol the outside of the jail. All night there has been a crowd of people about the jail, gathered by curiosity to see what might happen.

At midnight a force from Ludlow, armed in all conceivable ways, called at the jail and demanded the release of Hicks, but the Marshal refused. No organized attack was made, but a few shots were fired and great excitement was aroused for a time. The Marshal at 12:35 thought the Ludlow force would peaceably withdraw.

LATER.—Reports from Covington at 11:15, say the crowd is dispersing, and there is every indication that there will be no further trouble to-night.

Getting Rid of a Bad Crowd.

A Colored "Majah" in Jeopardy.
CINCINNATI, March 19.—A colored man who calls himself "Major" Hicks was to-day found guilty of murder in the first degree in Covington, Kentucky, and the jury fixed the penalty at death. He is the man who brutally murdered Henry Williams at Ludlow, Kentucky, some two or three months ago. The circumstances of the murder were so cold-blooded that a determined effort was made at the time to lynch Hicks, which was only prevented by the bravery of the officers at the Covington jail. Williams was an ex-emplary young man, in the employ of the Cincinnati Southern railroad, and was killed for the purpose of robbery.

A Sanctimonious Scoundrel.

A SACRED CONSTITUTION.

WHEELING, March 19.—Quite a local sensation occurred here to-day, caused by the sudden disappearance of John H. Zevely, publisher of a whilom paper known as the Postoffice Bulletin, published semi-occasionally, and largely devoted to advertising the business of Zevely, which was that of a stencil and die cutter, mainly for use in the post-offices of the country. It was found that he has been engaged in forging in a small way for a long time past, using the names of several citizens quite freely for accommodation on banks. He had hypothecated one or two bonds isud by the Lutheran church, of which he was a member, and had forged signatures to them. He was not a man of any known bad habits, and at one time stood quite high in his church. For some time past, however, he has been regarded with suspicion. Revolting Case of Infanticide.

CINCINNATI, March 19.—"Came to its death from being stabbed by its mother. I further find that said wounds were inflicted to commit murder." The above is the verdict of the coroner this afternoon in a case of infanticide. The mother is named Matilda Streazle. The birth and infanticide occurred two weeks ago, but the discovery of the child in the privy vault was not made until last night, and then accidentally by plumbers. Twenty mortal stabs were found on its body. The mother this afternoon testified that she gave birth to the child alone in the privy, knifed it to death to still its cries, threw it into the vault to conceal her shame, but says that she was mentally deranged. She is twenty-one years old, came from Germany to Chicago a year ago, and to this city about a month ago. She and Carl Seibel, the reputed father, were arrested for murder. GORE, O., Dec. 28.—At 6:30 o'clock this evening an unknown man opened the door of the house of Mrs. Manley Terrell, a widow living on the outskirts of this place, and shot her through the heart. Her two grown daughters were in the room at the time, but can give no description of the murderer, the deed being so quickly done and it being dark. Mrs. Terrell was the mother of William Terrell, the young man now serving a life term in the Ohio Penitentiary for the triple murder of the Weldon family near this place four years ago. There is no clew to the murderer. Vigilance committees have been organized and are scouring the country.

C., January 19.—Miss Ressie Werts, daughter of William Werts, living near Prosperity, Newberry county, this State, was brutally outraged and murdered Monday evening while going from her brother's house to her home. Spearman was shot to death on the spot where the crime was committed. Fair made his escape, but was recaptured today near Prosperity and hanged by a crowd of whites and blacks. The unfortunate victim was twenty-two years old, and a beautiful and excellent young woman.

The Scramble in New Jersey.

TRENTON, N. J., January 19.—A senatorial caucus to nominate a United States senator was held to-night. General Sewell was nominated on the twelfth ballots. Two ballots were declared irregular during the proceedings, more than 49 votes, the whole number, being cast. Tremendous excitement and confusion prevailed. Sewell's opponents were Robeson, Palsey, Parker, Dudley and Hobart. Sewell received 27 votes on the last ballot, and was declared elected. Robeson received 14 votes on several ballots, which was the highest given to any of Sewell's opponents. Sewell received 14 votes on the first ballot and increased gradually until he won the fight.

COLUMBUS, O., January 19.—A memorial signed by every Republican member of the general assembly, recommending Governor Foster for a position in the cabinet of the new regime, was forwarded to General Garfield to-day. Governor Foster and his most intimate friends were not consulted in this matter and are much chagrined at what they term the work of ill-advised friends. Governor Foster has written to General Garfield to assure him that the memorial does not meet with his approval, and that he must not be held responsible for it.

Accident on the Lake Shore Road.

CHICAGO, January 19.—There was a severe accident on the Lake Shore railroad, near Elkhart, Indiana, this morning, which resulted from gross carelessness, and might have been destructive of life. A freight-engine ran completely through the rear coach of the Chicago passenger-train, injuring Wm. Ravett, superintendent of bridges; cutting the head of Mrs. H. C. Wright, bruising Andrew Coder, and cutting Mrs. Kenyon. The small number of passengers alone averted a frightful accident.

CINCINNATI, January 19.—A special to the Gazette from Carlisle, Kentucky, says a body of masked men went to the house of Noah Anderson last night to punish him for maltreatment of his wife. Being refused admittance they broke down the door, when Anderson fired on them; they returned the fire and killing him instantly. His son, Samuel Anderson, came to his assistance, and he, too, was shot through the heart and instantly killed. No arrests have been made, but a man named Berry, in Carlisle, is suspected, he having a bad wound in the neck.

Dipthheria Raging in New Brunswick.

St. John, N. B. January 19.—Diphtheria is still raging in Grand Manan. John Meggs recently lost eight children by the terrible scourge within a few days.

CARLISLE, Ky., January 20.—On the Mavsville Branch of the Kentucky Central Railroad, about one and a half miles east of this place, and just below what is known as the Small Tunnel, is situated a small, one story log and frame house, the front portion being log, and the L., a new addition, being frame. Here for seventeen years Noah Anderson has lived and carried on the occupation of a farmer.

Mr. Anderson retired as usual with his family on last night, but before the morning's dawn he lay cold and stark in death, his fifteen-year old son, Samnel Anderson, lying in the same room pierced through and through with a fatal bullet. The circumstances of the killing of the father and the probable fatal wounding of the son is are follows:

About half-past ten o'clock a party of masked men, numbering some six or seven, were seen riding up the Cassaday branch in the direction of Anderson's, a married son of Noah Anderson, and who lives a short distance from his father. Arriving at Robert Anderson's the mob called him to the door, and, as he says, demanded that money he had of his father. He replied that he had none, when after some further conversation, interspersed with threats, they told him that would do, and started in the direction of Noah Anderson's, and, as is supposed, arriving there they called him to come out, when they proceeded to force the door, and finally succeeded. As the door flew open Mr. Anderson was standing near it with his pistols in his hands, and whether he or the mob fired first is not known. However, at that point some five or six shots were fired in rapid succession.
Mr. Anderson fell back mortally wounded. The ball, which was fired from a pistol, entered two and one-half inches above and one and one-half back of the right nipple, and, passing through the body, emerged about ten inches below the left armpit, evidently passing near, and perhaps wounding, the heart. He died almost instantly.
After being shot, Samuel Anderson, who, with a smaller brother, was sleeping in the room with his father, caught his father, and while supporting him received a fatal bullet in his own body. He was shot with a 38-calibre pistol.

The bark Ibis, from Pensacola, lay yesterday at the foot of Seventeenth street, North river. A Sun reporter boarded her and asked Captain Sawyer if he had really seen whales off Pimlico Sound on his way up the coast last Saturday.

"Whales?" said the genial Captain, "Any number of them. There must have been two miles of black backs and water-spouts."

Capt. Sawyer unrolled a time-worn chart on the table in his cabin and with his dividers followed down a number of pencil marks to latitude 40 degrees and longitude 74 degrees 15 minutes. This brought him to a point about eighty miles off Pimlico Sound, and further northeast of Cape Hatteras.

"It was on Saturday and Sunday, he continued, "when we encountered these sperm whales going south of southwest, as if to go around Hatteras. They were going very slowly, backs above the water, and were spouting all of the time. They were strolling along in groups, sunning themselves half an hour at a time, and then taking a header and coming up to spout."

"How many were there?"

"Well, first we met two schools of about 100 each, I should say. Occasionally they frolicked and flopped about heavily in a sort of dignified and elephantine sport. More followed, and the next morning (Sunday) we saw more. Altogether there were over 700 on the picnic. We passed within 500 feet of two big fellows, but they seemed preoccupied and didn't notice the ship. I don't think they knew we were there."

"Had you any means of capturing them?"

"No, and it did seem a pity to have so much valuable sperm oil indolently swimming away from us. There were some big whales there, too. I said to Limerick, one of my men here, 'Now there's a fellow that's worth $2000,' and he must have been, and there were bigger ones in the school. It would have been a harvest for a whaling ship. A million dollars in sperm whales is too good a haul to let go by, but we couldn't do anything. Occasionally I have seen a

sperm whale cruising along as far south as Savannah, and once in a while I've heard of whale ships off about there. But I never saw so many whales at one time before anywhere."

"Where were they going?"
"For squids, probably. That's a favorite food with them."

"Is there any danger to be feared from them?"
"No; they're harmless. I think I never heard of more than one case where a whale attacked a vessel, and that's in ancient history. Over a hundred years ago, I believe, the ship Easex was run down by a mad whale. My own experience with whales has been that they are shy, and if they upset a boat, do it by accident in trying to get away."

OKOLONA, MISS.

A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color.

OKOLONA, July 30.—About three weeks ago Robert Barker, colored, wilfully murdered Luther White, colored, about four miles from here. Barker went to White's house, and, without any notice or cause whatever, knocked him once or twice in the head with a club, spattering his brains over the floor. The murderer, not satisfied, then took his knife and ripped White's abdomen open. Barker has been at large until yesterday, when he was brought into town by a crowd that had been on the lookout for him ever since he committed the deed, and delivered to the proper authorities. To-day the officer, with a guard, started with him to the county jail in Houston, which is about twenty miles from here. When about six miles from town they were met by an armed mob, who seized the prisoner, carried him a short distance into the woods and shot him dead. Barker pleaded earnestly for his life, but without effect. Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color.

WEDNESDAY : JANUARY, 26, 1881

THE TENNESSEE JAIL AND INSANE ASYLUM SYSTEM.

We have received a copy of "the report of the committee of the State Board of Health on the prisons and public charities of the State of Tennessee," a paper of interest and value to the christian, and the philanthropist, and the sanatarian, and which is worthy of the thoughtful attention of every citizen of the State. Its details are not extensive, but, as far as it goes, we are glad to see that the report, as a whole, is creditable to the efforts of this State to punish wrong-doers with a fair regard to their claims as fellow-creatures. There are some spots in the picture, as we shall see in glancing over it. The commissioners began their task by sending eleven questions to the sheriff and prison officials for every county in the State—how many prisons there are we are not told, an omission we regret. The questions relate to the size of the jails, cells, etc., the number of prisoners, the ventilation, the heating, employment of the prisoners, the ratio of deaths and the causes, what epidemics, the water supply, how excrement is removed, how cleaning and disinfecting are arranged for, and of what material each jail is constructed. It is mortifying, and not very creditable to the sheriffs and officials, to learn that out of the whole only twenty-five replies were returned and they defective, and it is not pleasant to find that Memphis was one of the places that omitted filling up the papers sent to them by the commissioners. The legislature should make attention to a matter of this kind a duty, entailing a fine for a neglect to perform it. The meager returns received report that prisoners are humanely treated; food and wholesome water plenty; ventilation often through cracks and crevices of ill-constructed log houses; jails rarely over-crowded; the heating is from stoves, and, in two cases, by a furnace; generally open buckets in the cells for receiving and removing excrements; no epidemic for the last five years; and the mortality for the same time less than ten in a thousand. The jails are often insecure, and the frequent escapes lead to lynching. The answer to the question as to the occupations of the prisoners is one few readers will guess—it is card-playing! A very likely means of reclaiming the erring and reforming the vicious, of course, but the State has left the evil-doers to provide their own occupy work, no books or newspapers, only "devil's prayer-books." Tracts for Japan and China, and playing-cards for our own prisons—well done, christians of Tennessee? Labor and libraries might have a good effect upon habits and morals, but the prisoners are provided with neither. The report gives a description of Davidson county jail, which shows it to be a model one, and the same is said by Dr. Thornton of the Memphis jail, which, in the absence of a report, he personally examined. Crude as many of the Tennessee jails may be, aided by cracks and crevices, they are in a better sanitary condition, the commissioner's report says, "than any in the Union;" they are "more healthy than secure." There is little sickness and seldom a death. The State penitentiary, unfortunately, is destitute of the better characteristics, but its branch jails in various places where the convicts are set to work, are healthful and decent, though rough. In the penitentiary the want of space compels placing two, and even three, persons in cells constructed for only one. The following is horrible: "From the shops below to the wall is very nearly all 'made earth' from the excrements of the convicts and the offal of the kitchen. A pit is dug for the night-soil, which, when filled, is covered over from shavings from the shops and ashes from the furnaces. This soil comprises about one-half the inclosure. Near the stable and laundry and the females' water-closets is the well from which the prisoners get cool drinking water in the summer." The interior of the jail has no provision for ventilation, and air is breathed that is charged with carbonic acid and with the emanations of the open excrement bucket in each cell. The "made-earth" in the yards adds its quota of poison to this black-hole compound. The church prays "for all prisoners and captives;" a little doing as well as praying are wanted here. A drain conducts the soluble portions of the night-soil to a stream which flows through the center of the city, and when the cholera breaks out in Nashville there is the starting place. The diet of the convicts is good, and the officials are faithful and zealous and attend well to the cleanliness of the place, as far as its deficiencies will permit. Robbery of Registered Letters.

Robbery of Registered Letters.

CHICAGO, January 24.—Four days ago the postoffice authorities here were surprised by finding a registered letter pouch from Rochester, New York, had been cut open and seventeen out of twenty-one valuable packages stolen. As five of the envelopes bore Robinson postoffice stamps, a telegram was sent there to ascertain their contents, and it was found that one contained ten dollars, three others five dollars each, and the fifth a ruby breastpin. From this Special Henshaw deduces that the total loss, which was at first rumored to be $150,000, does not exceed $200. The bag came over the Michigan Southern road, but whether the robbery took place on the train at the depot or in the Chicago postoffice is not known. The matter was kept a close secret by the postoffice authorities, in the hope of detecting the robbers.

HER CHANCES ARE GOOD.

LYNCHBURG, VA., January 24.—Suit has been brought in the United States district court in behalf of Millie T. Whitlow, a white girl living in Cumberland county. Miss Whitlow, it appears, has lived for some time in the family of a negro, as nurse and house servant, being treated and considered as one of the household, though nothing specific was alleged as to criminal conduct or character. This mode of life tended to injure her reputation in the neighborhood. After leaving the house of Coleman, the negro, the girl entered one of the public schools of the county as pupil, upon which the rest of the scholars all stopped attending it. The teacher applied for instructions to the school board, and was directed to exclude Miss Whitlow. He did so, and she now brings suit for damages, naming a round sum. All parties to the suit are white, but the girl lost her character by living with the negro as his servant. As this fact gives the Federal court jurisdiction it will be a point of no small importance. Alexander Rives, who recently caused the indictment of the State judges for failure to put negroes on their juries, will preside at the trial.

Brooks and the Burglar.

CHICAGO, January 24.—One of the boldest and most successful burglaries ever planned and executed in this city occurred about 7 o'clock last evening, at the office of the South Chicago Iron and Steel Works, on Ashland avenue, near Thirtieth street, but was not reported by the police until 2 o'clock this morning. It was then learned that three masked burglars had forced the office door, bound and gagged the janitor, Chas. Brooks, and while one of them stood guard over him with a pistol, the others drilled a hole in the safe, blew open the combination, and bidding the old watchman a cheerful good night, left, taking $1000 in five-dollar gold pieces, and $150 in coin, together with about $9000 in bills, done up in envelopes, ready for paying the help to-day. The above facts are given by Brooks, but the police regard something about the affair as sufficiently suspicious to implicate him, and have accordingly arrested him and his son. He told somewhat contradictory stories; his unruffled clothing and unprepossessing appearance raised doubts of his accuracy and integrity. Paddy Cavanaugh, a notorious character, was also arrested.
